country.name: Türkiye
country.tagline: The world's sixth-largest vineyard, almost all for eating, with a small and stubborn wine scene built on Öküzgözü, Boğazkere, Kalecik Karası and Emir.

stats.note: OIV 2025: 395 kha of vines, the sixth largest vineyard in the world, but mostly table grapes and raisins (Sultaniye); only a small share of the crop, estimated at 3 to 15 percent, is made into wine. Wine output below the OIV's 1 mhl reporting threshold.

country.overview:
Anatolia is one of the places where the grapevine was domesticated, and wine runs through its ancient history: Hittite laws of the second millennium BC fined anyone who damaged a vineyard, Assyrian merchants at Kültepe traded wine, the Phrygians and Lydians shipped it across the Aegean, and the Ionian coast was Dionysus's home ground. Under the Ottomans, commercial winemaking was the business of non-Muslim communities (Greeks, Armenians, Syriacs and Jews), and the population exchanges and expulsions of the early twentieth century took much of that knowledge with them.

The Republic restarted the industry from the top. Atatürk ordered a state winery at Tekirdağ in 1925, the Tekel monopoly controlled alcohol for most of the century, and the private houses that still dominate, Doluca (1926) and Kavaklıdere (1929), date from those years. Tekel's wine division was privatised in 2004 (its successor, Kayra, owns the historic Buzbağ brand), and a wave of new estates in Thrace, on the Aegean and in Cappadocia began replanting native grapes alongside Cabernet and Merlot. There are now roughly 140 licensed wineries.

The native grapes are the reason to pay attention. Öküzgözü ('ox eye') from Elazığ is juicy and bright; Boğazkere ('throat-scratcher') from Diyarbakır is dark and tannic, and the two together are the classic Turkish red blend. Kalecik Karası, rescued by Ankara University in the 1960s and 1970s from near extinction, makes pale, perfumed, Pinot-like reds near Ankara. Emir grows on the volcanic tuff of Cappadocia and gives crisp, mineral whites and traditional-method sparkling; Narince, from Tokat, gives fuller whites. On the Aegean, Urla Karası and Bornova Misketi have been brought back from near extinction.

The obstacle is policy. Since a 2013 law, alcohol advertising and promotion are banned, producers cannot advertise or even show their wines in most media, sales are restricted at night and near schools and mosques, and special consumption tax is among the highest in Europe and is revised upward regularly. Domestic consumption is tiny (about one litre per person a year), so the industry lives from tourism, the urban middle class and a small export trade.

history.title: Wine in the Assyrian colony at Kültepe
history.text: Clay tablets from the Old Assyrian merchant colony at Kültepe (Kanesh), near Kayseri, record wine among the goods traded across Anatolia.

history.title: Hittite vineyard laws
history.text: Hittite law codes from Hattusa set penalties for damaging vineyards and ritual texts describe wine libations to the gods.

history.title: Atatürk's state winery
history.text: The new Republic ordered a state winery at Tekirdağ in Thrace; Tekel later held the alcohol monopoly.

history.title: Doluca and Kavaklıdere
history.text: The two private houses that still lead the industry were founded in Thrace (Doluca at Mürefte) and Ankara (Kavaklıdere).

history.title: Tekel's wine business privatised
history.text: The state monopoly's alcoholic drinks division was privatised; its wineries became Kayra, and a generation of boutique estates followed.

history.title: The alcohol advertising ban
history.text: Law 6487 banned alcohol advertising and promotion and restricted retail sales between 22:00 and 06:00, sharply limiting how Turkish wineries can reach customers.

country.classification: Türkiye has no operational appellation system for wine comparable to the EU's; labels name grapes, wineries and broad regions (Thrace, Aegean, Cappadocia, Eastern Anatolia). A few geographical indications exist for grapes and other products, and producer groups such as Thrace's 'Trakya' wine route promote regional identity.
country.climate_soils: Four broad zones: maritime Thrace and the Marmara coast; the Mediterranean Aegean coast and its hotter inland plateaus (Denizli, Manisa); continental Central Anatolia at 800 to 1,200 metres, including Cappadocia's volcanic tuff, where growers sometimes bury vines against winter frost; and the hot, dry, high Euphrates valley of Eastern Anatolia (Elazığ, Malatya, Diyarbakır).

grapes.name: Öküzgözü
grapes.note: Elazığ's 'ox-eye' red: juicy, bright, low tannin.

grapes.name: Boğazkere
grapes.note: Diyarbakır's tannic, dark red; blended with Öküzgözü in Buzbağ and many modern reds.

grapes.name: Kalecik Karası
grapes.note: Pale, perfumed red from the Kızılırmak valley near Ankara, revived from near extinction.

grapes.name: Emir
grapes.note: Cappadocia's crisp white, still and sparkling.

grapes.name: Narince
grapes.note: Fuller white from Tokat, also used for stuffed vine leaves.

grapes.name: Sultaniye
grapes.note: The seedless raisin grape of Manisa and Denizli, mostly for drying.

further_reading: Turkish Wine: The Complete Guide (various), and the work of Jancis Robinson and Julia Harding on Turkish varieties
Wine Grapes, Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025

regions.name: Thrace and Marmara
regions.tagline: European Türkiye between three seas: the industry's historic base.
regions.summary: Thrace and the Marmara coast make 30 to 40 percent of Turkish wine. Mürefte and Şarköy on the Sea of Marmara were Greek wine villages before 1923; Doluca and Kayra work there, and new estates (Chamlija, Arcadia, Barbare, Şato Kalpak, Gülor) planted Kırklareli and the Gelibolu peninsula from the 2000s.
regions.history: The Tekirdağ state winery of 1925 and Doluca (1926) began the Republic's wine industry here.
regions.terroir: Maritime climate moderated by the Aegean, the Marmara and the Black Sea; clay and limestone hills.
regions.grapes: Papazkarası, Yapıncak, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025

regions.name: Aegean
regions.tagline: The largest wine region by volume: Urla, Bozcaada, Denizli and Manisa.
regions.summary: The Aegean region makes around a third of Turkish wine. The coast has revived old Greek-era vineyards at Urla near İzmir and on the island of Bozcaada (ancient Tenedos); the inland plateaus of Denizli (especially Çal) and Manisa grow most of the country's Sultaniye and the rosé grape Çalkarası.
regions.history: Smyrna (İzmir) was the Ottoman Empire's great export port for wine and raisins in the seventeenth century.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean coast and higher inland plateaus at 600 to 850 metres.
regions.grapes: Urla Karası, Bornova Misketi, Karalahna, Kuntra, Çavuş, Çalkarası, Sultaniye, international varieties.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025

regions.name: Central Anatolia and Cappadocia
regions.tagline: Volcanic tuff, cave cellars and Emir; Kalecik Karası near Ankara.
regions.summary: Cappadocia's tuff landscape, with vineyards at 1,000 to 1,200 metres around Ürgüp, Uçhisar and Göreme, has stored wine in rock-cut cellars for centuries. Its white grape Emir makes crisp still and sparkling wines; Kalecik, north-east of Ankara, is the home of Kalecik Karası. Kavaklıdere and Vinkara (Kalecik) and the Cappadocian houses Turasan and Kocabağ are the main producers.
regions.history: Cappadocia had a large Greek Orthodox population, exchanged in 1924; villages such as Mustafapaşa (Sinasos) still have their wine cellars.
regions.terroir: Continental, 800 to 1,200 metres, cold winters (vines are sometimes buried), volcanic tuff and sand.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025

regions.name: Eastern and Southeastern Anatolia
regions.tagline: The Euphrates highlands of Öküzgözü and Boğazkere, and Syriac wine in Mardin.
regions.summary: Elazığ and Malatya in the upper Euphrates valley are the heartland of Öküzgözü; the Diyarbakır plain grows Boğazkere. Most grapes are trucked west to wineries in Thrace and Ankara. In Mardin, the Syriac Christian community keeps a small tradition with the grape Mazrona.
regions.history: Kayra's Elazığ winery, inherited from Tekel, produces Buzbağ, the classic Öküzgözü and Boğazkere blend.
regions.terroir: Continental high plateaus at 900 to 1,200 metres, hot dry summers, cold winters.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025

sites.name: Kavaklıdere winery
sites.text: Founded in Ankara in 1929 and now based at Akyurt north-east of the capital, Kavaklıdere is Türkiye's largest private wine producer, with vineyards in Cappadocia, the Aegean and Thrace; its Pendore and Çankaya brands are national classics.

sites.name: Vinkara, Kalecik
sites.text: A winery in Kalecik on the Kızılırmak, near the village that gave its name to Kalecik Karası; known for still and traditional-method sparkling Kalecik Karası.

sites.name: Turasan winery, Ürgüp
sites.text: A Cappadocian family winery founded in 1943 in Ürgüp with cellars cut into the tuff; makes Emir, Narince and Öküzgözü.

sites.name: Kocabağ, Uçhisar
sites.text: Family winery at Uçhisar in Cappadocia, beside the fairy chimneys of Göreme, specialising in Emir and local reds.

sites.name: Urla Şarapçılık
sites.text: Can Ortabaş's winery on the Urla peninsula west of İzmir, which led the revival of the near-extinct Urla Karası and of Aegean vineyards abandoned after 1923.

sites.name: Corvus Vineyards, Bozcaada
sites.text: Architect Reşit Soley's estate on Bozcaada (ancient Tenedos), working the island's Karalahna and Çavuş alongside international grapes.

sites.name: Doluca, Mürefte
sites.text: Founded in 1926 by Nihat Kutman at Mürefte on the Sea of Marmara, once a Greek wine village; Doluca introduced many international varieties to Türkiye.

sites.name: Chamlija
sites.text: Mustafa Çamlıca's estate in Büyükkarıştıran, Kırklareli, one of the leading boutique wineries of Thrace, known for Papazkarası and blends.

sites.name: Hattusa
sites.text: The Hittite capital, whose archives include laws protecting vineyards and texts on wine offerings; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sites.name: Kültepe (Kanesh)
sites.text: The Bronze Age city and Assyrian merchant colony near Kayseri whose tablets record trade in wine around 1900 BC.
